---
title: "4. Show uncertainty"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

- Uncertainty should be incorporated visually when possible
  - Confidence intervals and standard errors should be included for model estimates / predictions

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si.dta", clear

// 4.a - Add 95% confidence intervals to the bar chart
mean cesd if year == 2022, over(dayweekdrink)

marginsplot, recast(bar) plotopts(barwidth(.5) col(*.7)) ciopts(col(gs8)) ///
    ytitle("Depressive symptoms") ylabel(0(0.5)2) ///
    xtitle("Days drinking alcohol per week") ///
    title("[4.a] Average number of depressive symptoms") ///
    subtitle("By number of days drinking per week (95% confidence intervals)")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-04_a-bar_y_CIs.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-04_a-bar_y_CIs.png){width=80% fig-alt="[4.a] Bar chart of the average number of depressive symptoms by days drinking alcohol per week (0 to 7), with 95% confidence intervals: the average is highest at 0 days (about 1.7), lowest at 6 days (about 1.0), and between 1.2 and 1.3 for the other numbers of days; the intervals are widest for 4 to 6 days."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[4.a] Bar chart of the average number of depressive symptoms by days drinking alcohol per week (0 to 7), with 95% confidence intervals: the average is highest at 0 days (about 1.7), lowest at 6 days (about 1.0), and between 1.2 and 1.3 for the other numbers of days; the intervals are widest for 4 to 6 days."
library(foreign)            # load Stata datasets
library(ggplot2)            # main graphics package
library(dplyr)              # data manipulation tools
library(cleanplots)         # Mize's graphics scheme

## Use cleanplots colors, markers, lines, and theme for all graphs ##
cleanplots_defaults()
theme_update(plot.title.position = "plot")   # titles start at left edge of graph

# Health and Retirement Study Data
hrs <- read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si.dta")

# 4.a - Add 95% confidence intervals to the bar chart (2022 wave)
ggplot(filter(hrs, year == 2022), aes(x = dayweekdrink, y = cesd)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar", fill = cleanplots_colors("ltblue", bars = TRUE),
               width = .7) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = "errorbar", width = .3, color = "gray50") +
  labs(x = "Days drinking alcohol per week",
       y = "Depressive symptoms",
       title = "[4.a] Average number of depressive symptoms",
       subtitle = "By number of days drinking per week (95% confidence intervals)") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2, 0.5)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2))
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// 4.b - Recreate plot above but with a dot plot
marginsplot, recast(scatter) recastci(rspike) ciopt(col(*.5)) ///
    ytitle("Depressive symptoms") ylabel(0(0.5)2) ///
    xtitle("Days drinking alcohol per week") ///
    title("[4.b] Average number of depressive symptoms") ///
    subtitle("By number of days drinking per week (95% confidence intervals)")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-04_b-dot_y_CIs.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-04_b-dot_y_CIs.png){width=80% fig-alt="[4.b] The same averages and 95% confidence intervals as a dot plot: a dot at each average with a vertical line for its confidence interval."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[4.b] The same averages and 95% confidence intervals as a dot plot: a dot at each average with a vertical line for its confidence interval."
# 4.b - Recreate plot above but with a dot plot
ggplot(filter(hrs, year == 2022), aes(x = dayweekdrink, y = cesd)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = "linerange", alpha = .5) +
  labs(x = "Days drinking alcohol per week",
       y = "Depressive symptoms",
       title = "[4.b] Average number of depressive symptoms",
       subtitle = "By number of days drinking per week (95% confidence intervals)") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 2, 0.5)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2))
```

:::

### Bad graph levity

![](images/error-bars-tweet.png){width=50% fig-alt="Tweet: Wait a second, these are not real error bars ... the author literally just put the letter T above the bar graphs, above a bar chart whose error bars are the letter T."}

## Moving forward: building blocks

*"There is a strand of the data viz world that argues everything could be a bar chart. That's possibly true but also possibly a world without joy."* *(Amanda Cox, Editor, The Upshot, quoted in [HBR 2013](https://hbr.org/2013/03/power-of-visualizations-aha-moment))*

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
- As we move into more advanced data and model visualizations the basic tools we learned in this section will often reappear
- Aspects of both bar charts and dot plots are used very often in displaying complex model results
  - They both have good visualization properties and work nicely as the building blocks of more complicated graphs---where you can layer on additional aspects
:::
